items.title: AI is forcing us to pay off 40 years of technical debt
items.content:
In late October, a slew of major cybersecurity issues came to light. But none were bigger than the so-called PHP2Shell vulnerability , which put a plethora of websites, including those of NASA , Wikipedia , the White House, and all other sites that run on Wordpress or Drupal (among others) at risk of exploits capable of both reading sensitive data and running malicious code on the host server.

As far as anyone is aware, disaster has been averted: The hack was discovered by cybersecurity researchers who reported it to the PHP Foundation, and a patch was released before any bad actors got their hands on the exploit. However, PHP2Shell may be the canary in the coal mine, serving as a warning sign for what’s to come in the age of AI.

“One of the things we’re witnessing now is that all the legacy software that was written by humans over the last 40 years is being exposed,” says Matt Suiche , AI security research lead at the cybersecurity startup Tolmo . “Now it is time for the technical debt to be paid off.”

PHP, which originally stood for “personal home page,” is a programming language created back in 1994 and largely used by legacy sites. The bug underlying the PHP2Shell vulnerability was reported to the PHP Foundation as far back as 2024. The bug caused a common type of issue called an out-of-memory error, in which the amount of memory allocated to a piece of data is too small to hold the data. Normally, this type of error causes the program to crash—an unpleasant but not inherently dangerous result. And so the bug remained unaddressed.

“If you look at any at any point of time, there will be a bunch of bug reports that are waiting to be fixed, which are just crashes. Most people don’t take them very seriously,” says Suman Jana , an associate professor of computer science at Columbia University .

“It’s just that it’s a lot of very specific reasoning that is painful to do. And AI, I think, has done a very good job at that.” –Suman Jana, Columbia University

Earlier this year, the cybersecurity firm Calif offered to independently audit PHP, sponsored by OpenAI . Within two weeks, a researcher at Calif, aided by AI tools, found a way to use the out-of-memory bug to run arbitrary code on the host server, allowing a malicious actor to install malware or read critical data. Now, it was no longer a minor bug—it was a critical vulnerability, and the Calif team alerted the PHP foundation to start working on a patch immediately.

Jana says actually exploiting the bug requires carefully working out a way to jump to a specific point in the memory for a particular program running on the server, and work out exactly which bits to overwrite in what order to gain control of the system. “It’s not really rocket science,” he says. “It’s just that it’s a lot of very specific reasoning that is painful to do. And AI, I think, has done a very good job at that.”

To be clear, the researchers at Calif (as well as OpenAI and Wiz, a cybersecurity company that confirmed and expanded the vulnerabilities) had deep knowledge of both cybersecurity and the PHP language. “I’m not claiming that AI can do it all by itself. It clearly cannot,” Jana says. “But it is improving a lot, so the top 0.1 percent [of experts] can get a lot more stuff done, and also just below the 0.1 percent now will be able to go there without understanding all the nitty-gritty details.”

AI Tools and Formal Verification in Security

After the exploits were disclosed to the PHP Foundation, a team of four engineers spent two months developing a patch to release as quickly as possible.

“There is a fundamental asymmetry in finding bugs and fixing bugs,” Jana says. “Because when you’re fixing bugs you have to make sure that you know all parts of that attack are closed, and also that you don’t break any existing functionality.”

items.title: So my ISP was hijacking my DNS
items.summary: networking
items.content:
It was just a boring Saturday afternoon, and I thought I'd fix some of the problems with my homelab. One of those problems was that an external site my Podman container was trying to talk to just wasn't working.

I kept getting "Site cannot be reached" almost immediately. This made me suspect something was wrong with my DNS setup, so I started doing a dig on the domain. I tried different providers, Google DNS, Cloudflare, pretty much everyone. Almost all of them returned the same IP address. But as soon as I tried Cloudflare's DoH endpoint, I got a completely different IP address.

I took the IP I got from the first DNS resolution and tried to look up who owned it. Lo and behold, it was my goddamn ISP. That's when I realised my ISP was hijacking my DNS queries and returning a tampered IP address.

Well, the obvious answer was DoT (DNS over TLS) or DoH (DNS over HTTPS). I made a tweet about this, and it somehow blew up .

But going through the replies, I noticed quite a few misconceptions and questions that I couldn't answer one by one.

So I figured I'd use this article to address some of those questions and clear up a few misconceptions along the way.

For those of you who don't know, Unbound is basically a DNS resolver, kind of like what Cloudflare runs at 1.1.1.1 . The difference is, you can run it locally. It works by querying DNS servers to figure out the IP address for a domain, starting at the root nameservers and eventually making its way to the domain's authoritative nameserver.

Now here's the catch. DNS resolution doesn't happen over a single connection. Your resolver might have to talk to multiple nameservers to figure out an IP address, and these queries are traditionally sent over plaintext DNS, usually UDP. Which means, you guessed it, your ISP can snoop on or even tamper with your DNS traffic.

But you can also configure a forward-zone in Unbound. Instead of resolving DNS queries itself, Unbound can forward them to another DNS resolver. And if that resolver supports DoT, the connection to it is encrypted, which means your ISP can't casually snoop on or tamper with your DNS queries in transit.

It's understandable why someone would assume DNSSEC is what protects them here. I mean, it has DNS and Security right in the name. And in a way, it does, but it works through verification, not encryption.

You see, DNSSEC doesn't encrypt your DNS traffic before sending it to a resolver. It uses cryptographic signatures to verify that the DNS data is authentic and hasn't been tampered with. But the problem here remains the same: your DNS traffic is still unencrypted in transit. Which means, your ISP can still snoop on it or mess with the responses.

And for DNSSEC validation to work, the domain you're querying needs to have DNSSEC properly configured, with valid signatures and a chain of trust. And here's another problem: according to the October 2026 Defaults.Exposed census , only 7.03% of graded domains have a valid, fully validating DNSSEC chain.

If a tampered response fails DNSSEC validation, your resolver will return SERVFAIL instead of handing you that bogus IP address.

And yes, this is true. DoT and DoH rely on you trusting the DNS resolver you're sending your queries to. They encrypt the connection, so your ISP can't casually snoop on or tamper with your DNS traffic in transit. But that doesn't mean the resolver itself can't mess with your responses. You're still putting your trust in whoever runs that DNS server.

Indeed. Although your regular internet traffic is encrypted with TLS, your ISP can see the hostname during the TLS handshake (SNI). They can also figure out which site you're visiting just from the destination IP sometimes.

Unless, of course, you tunnel your traffic through a VPN. I use Mullvad through Tailscale's exit node feature.

Of course, this just shifts some of the trust to your VPN provider. But that's a story for another day.

items.title: Residential Proxies Detected on White House Network
items.content:
Our Residential Proxy Observatory , launched earlier this week, is a first-of-its-kind interface that gives researchers a global view of residential proxy and anonymized internet activity.

While our team was looking through it, we noticed residential proxy exit activity on AS2650 . AS2650 is registered to the Executive Office of the President, the federal agency that hosts the White House network. Residential proxy services sell access to everyday devices, letting customers send traffic through them so it appears to come from that device's network.

Confirmed residential proxy activity observed from the White House network, October 5 to November 3, 2026. What we observed

Our residential proxy enumeration pipeline exited through the White House network 236 separate times .

Those exits came from 6 addresses , on 26 of the 30 days .

28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.

To make sure this was not a fluke, we checked these addresses against other residential proxy detection services, such as Spur and Synthient. Their public IP context pages independently identify these addresses as residential proxy exits.

This is public access. Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.

Most of the activity happens in the evening, Eastern time: about half of it falls between 5 p.m. and midnight, and almost none happens in the early morning. That pattern suggests a person rather than a public guest Wi-Fi network: someone regularly on the White House network late into the evening, whose device is infected with a proxy SDK. Our data shows the exits, not the device or the person behind them.

Past research has shown that poorly secured proxy SDKs can allow internal network access and lateral movement. This is how past botnets have spread. In A Broken System Fueling Botnets , the researchers at Synthient documented how the Kimwolf botnet reached at least 2 million devices, mostly Android devices with an exposed ADB service, through residential proxy networks. If an SDK on this network has the same kind of flaw, anyone buying proxy access could use it to reach internal systems.

The White House is not the only surprise in the observatory. Residential proxies also reach some of the most isolated places on the planet.

Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha is the South Atlantic territory that includes the most remote inhabited island in the world. We recorded 413 addresses and more than 32,000 observations there, split between Starlink and the island's local internet provider, Sure Saint Helena.

We also recorded three observations from Antarctica . All of them come from a Cloudflare WARP address that points to McMurdo Station.

Pitcairn : 1 Starlink address, 1 observation.

Norfolk Island : 1 Norfolk Telecom address, 4 observations.

Svalbard : 1 Starlink address in Longyearbyen, 3 observations.

Also seen: the Falklands (388 addresses), the Chagos Islands (43), Tokelau (21) and South Georgia (7).

Residential proxies have infected every corner of the world, and it looks like there is no place they cannot reach. Layer3 Intel tracks residential proxy and anonymization infrastructure worldwide. Even when the proxies hide in networks on the farthest corners of the planet, we can still observe them, leaving threat actors no place to hide.

For relevant agencies: We have backed up the raw logs of the recorded activity and are willing to share them. You can request them through our contact page .

items.title: Eremias chagaiensis, racerunner lizard from the Chagai Desert, Pakistan
items.content:
Chagai Racerunner of Pakistan. Photo by Masroor, R., Danish, M. & Jablonski, D. (2026)

The lizard is named after Chagai District, where researchers documented it at four localities. It has a distinctive maze-like pattern of winding brown markings across its back.

Researchers have described a new species of racerunner lizard from the Chagai Desert in western Pakistan, near the borders of Afghanistan and Iran. The species, named Eremias chagaiensis , was identified during field surveys conducted between 2022 and 2025 in Balochistan.

The lizard is named after Chagai District, where researchers documented it at four localities. It has a distinctive maze-like pattern of winding brown markings across its back, unlike the longitudinal stripes typically seen in many related racerunners. Both juveniles and adults retain the patter. It is around 2.2 inches (5.7 cm) in length, with a tail that can exceed twice its body length.

Researchers used DNA analysis, along with comparisons of physical characteristics and scale patterns to establish that the lizard represents a new species. The researchers say it closely resembles Eremias graphica , a species described from Iran in 2023, but genetic analysis confirmed the two are separate evolutionary lineages.

“Balochistan’s deserts are among the least explored places in South Asia. Finding a new lizard here tells us how much is still undocumented,” lead researcher Rafaqat Masroor of the Pakistan Museum of Natural History said in a statement released to the media.

Eremias chagaiensis inhabits loose sand, particularly low dunes and sandy areas near desert shrubs, where it excavates burrows. Researchers did not find it on neighboring gravel plains, which were occupied by another racerunner, Eremias fasciata.

The study also confirms the presence of E. fasciata in Pakistan for the first time using modern specimens and DNA evidence. Although the species was reportedly recorded in Balochistan in 1921, its presence in the country had not been verified for more than a century.

Researchers currently know E. chagaiensis from just four locations. However, similar habitat extends into neighboring Afghanistan and possibly Iran, and additional surveys are needed to determine its full distribution. Because population numbers and potential threats remain unknown, researchers recommend a provisional conservation assessment of Data Deficient.

The findings bring the number of Eremias species documented in Pakistan to eight. The research was published in Zootaxa in a study by Rafaqat Masroor, Muhammad Danish, and Daniel Jablonski.

An abstract of the paper, “At the western edge of South Asia: a new species of Eremias Fitzinger, 1834 (Squamata: Lacertidae) from Balochistan and confirmed records of E. fasciata Blanford, 1874 for Pakistan” can be read on the Zootaxa website .

items.title: 사생활침해, 개인정보보호법 위반, 명예훼손, 사이버불링 정황 공론화
items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

items.title: Shlemiel the Painter Is Back: How Zig’s libc Rewrite Made SQLite Slower
items.summary: performance, rust, zig
items.content:
Back in 2001, Joel Spolsky – whose writings had a big influence my career – wrote a great piece titled Back to Basics . The premise of the piece is that practitioners should understand the basics: However abstract and remote we may seem from the basic algorithms that drive computing, they can unexpectedly have enormous consequences on our projects.

One of his examples is the “Shlemiel the Painter” trap, where a seemingly simple choice leads to quadratic runtime complexity. In that parable, a street line painter never moves his can of paint. As he gets further and further along in the line, increasingly more of his time is spent walking to and from his can of paint.

It is astonishing how often this Shlemiel the Painter pattern recurs 1 , including now in 2026.

My Chess Analysis Service Staggers Under Load

A few days ago I posted about a chess analysis service I put online ↗ 2 . This is primarily a Rust service backed by sqlite that dishes out analysis tasks to runners. Each runner processes upwards of hundreds of chess games and return a large set of JSON bundles back to the main service, where they are processed and then stuffed into sqlite.

While the analysis pegs two dozen cores on a runner for minutes on end, the process of storing the data should take milliseconds. Sub-milliseconds.

Imagine my surprise when on the first really large set of games, the simple process of inserting the JSON data – maybe about 40,000 records – into the data store took minutes . During all of my testing this never really appeared as a critical path, but with a large set of records it suddenly was a breaking problem.

What made this more perplexing was that it completely saturated a core, being a CPU-bound operation. How could inserting simple JSON into SQLite yield minutes of CPU time?

Shlemiel the painter has made an appearance. To drop a spoiler, he was introduced to the project via Zig’s cc compiler and its replacement for standard library functions.

A Minor Issue In Zig Becomes A Major Performance Issue

The project isn’t built in Zig, but instead uses Rust. The sqlx sqlite crate needs to be compiled for the target environment – sqlite is of course a C project – so to facilitate cross-platform building, generating both Mac ARM64 and Linux ARM64 / x86-64 binaries from this machine in a convenient build and deploy workflow, zig cc is used to compile sqlite when targeting Linux, generously offering up cross-platform targeting via cargo-zigbuild.

From one build and deploy script on my Mac I can target all of my platforms without containers or build machines. Zig’s elegant libzigc re-implements the standard library so you can static link the necessary functionality.

Zig uses musl (the standard library rewrite), but they have been rewriting it piece by piece in pure Zig (via libzigc), removing the C dependencies one at a time.

And that’s where the performance issue was introduced.

In the rewrite of strspn , replacing the musl version with the pure zig variant ), the first step measures the entire length of the string. This is also seen in the rewrites of strcspn, strpbrk and strstr.

This is a problem for tokenizers. A tokenizer takes a giant string and a common iterating step is to skip whitespace, getting the new string location and then repeating this pattern repeatedly. With this shlemiel the painter pattern introduced with these rewrites, as it steps through the text it is tokenizing it is remeasuring the entire length of the string endlessly.

This is what caused my performance issue, and it’s why it appeared on Linux but was never seen on my Mac (where zig wasn’t used for compiling sqlite).

Tokenizing a 1.2MB file, which was seen passing json to sqlite, is approximately 12,000x slower with this pattern. As the file gets larger, the slowdown is quadratic.

items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-115770 📢 Source: GitHub_M 💣 CVSS Score: 0.0 (NA) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: False Pocket ID is an OIDC provider that allows users to authenticate with their passkeys to services. From 2.2.0 until 2.12.0, SendEmailVerification uses the token model in backend/internal/model/email_verification_token.go to bind an email-verification token only to the user's identifier, while UpdateUser can change the account email without invalidating the outstanding token and VerifyEmail marks the current address as verified. An ordinary user can request a token for an address they control, change the account to an arbitrary unused address, and redeem the old token so Pocket ID publishes the new address with email_verified set to true. The default affected configuration uses emailsVerified=false and allowOwnAccountEdit=true; the target address must not already belong to another Pocket ID user. A relying application that trusts a verified email for automatic account matching or provisioning can link the attacker's identity to another user's account, while applications that rely exclusively on the stable OIDC sub claim are not affected by that downstream consequence. This issue is fixed in version 2.12.0. 📅 Published Date: 2026-11-04T22:32:18.097Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-115770

items.title: Nvidia RTX Spark encrypted firmware slows inference speed to 35% on Linux
items.content:
Can you run Linux on the Nvidia RTX Spark laptop?

Yes, but it comes with a serious catch. Linux installs and runs on RTX Spark laptops like the MSI Prestige N16 Flip AI Plus, including GPU acceleration through Nvidia’s open kernel driver. The problem is clock speed: once the laptop is plugged into wall power, the GPU gets locked to roughly 780 MHz on Linux instead of the 2 GHz-plus it hits on Windows. That turns a chip capable of around 65 tokens per second on a 120 billion parameter model into one struggling to break 14 tokens per second, for reasons tied to power management firmware that Linux currently can’t read.

Dual-booting Linux works on the MSI Prestige RTX Spark laptop, with a full desktop, GPU acceleration via Nvidia’s open driver, 4K output at 120Hz, and working audio, keyboard, and touchpad once configured correctly.

A hidden Windows-only component called the Nvidia Platform Controllers and Framework manages power delivery between CPU and GPU, and it has no Linux equivalent, which is the root cause of the slowdown.

GPU clock speed collapses to about 780 MHz on Linux when plugged in , compared to roughly 2.2 GHz on Windows, because the firmware’s power table is encrypted and only the Windows driver can decrypt it.

Benchmarks on GPT-OSS-120B show the gap clearly : Windows hit 65.4 tokens per second, WSL hit 65.1, the Nvidia DGX Spark hit 61, and native Linux on the same laptop managed only 13.9.

Memory allocation is a separate headache , since the laptop reserves 96GB of unified memory for the GPU by default and only Windows exposes a setting to change that split, which is required before Linux can see more than a sliver of RAM.

WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux) is the practical middle ground today , since it rides on the Windows driver stack and keeps full GPU boost whether the laptop is plugged in or on battery, while still running Linux-first AI tools like vLLM.

A real fix depends on Nvidia , specifically on porting the platform controller’s power management logic into its Linux driver, which would effectively turn the laptop into a portable version of the DGX Spark.

On-prem or in your private cloud. Remy and every app you build stay inside your walls.

The AI platform for building secure, compliant enterprise apps Try Remy today

What makes the RTX Spark laptop different from a normal Windows PC?

The RTX Spark platform, which ships in machines like the MSI Prestige, the Asus ProArt, and the Dell XPS, uses the same GPU design as Nvidia’s DGX Spark desktop unit. But where the DGX Spark ships with Nvidia’s own Linux build out of the box, every one of these laptop variants ships with Windows on ARM.

That distinction matters because Windows on ARM with CUDA support is new. ARM-based Windows machines have existed for a few years, but pairing that architecture with Nvidia’s CUDA stack only became possible with this chip. The laptops also support unified memory configurations up to 128GB, shared between CPU and GPU, which is unusual for a laptop and central to why they’re being marketed at AI developers in the first place.

Because so much of the AI tooling ecosystem, including vLLM and SGLang, is built Linux-first, developers who buy these machines naturally want to know whether they can ditch Windows, or at least dual-boot, without losing performance.

How do you actually install Linux on it?

The process is not plug-and-play. A first attempt using Omarchy (a Linux distribution with Arch roots) failed because, while it already supported the chip on Asus and Dell hardware, the MSI Prestige behaved differently, producing a flickering, unstable display during boot.

Switching to Debian worked more reliably, but still needed workarounds. The installer couldn’t connect to Wi-Fi, so installation required a USB Ethernet adapter. Out of the box, Debian also didn’t recognize the keyboard, touchpad, or GPU, because none of the laptop-specific hardware support was present in a vanilla kernel.

items.title: Your Cryptography Conspiracy Theory Is Wrong
items.summary: cryptography
items.content:
This conversation plays out hundreds of times a day, but (thankfully) only a handful of those involve me:

Cryptography nerd: “Oh, you probably want to use [sensible recommendation].”

Person: “Ah, well, can I really trust that? The NSA probably backdoored it 30 years ago. Dual_EC, amirite?!”

Koblitz and Menezes, unheard: “ You fucking wot m8? “

Conspiracy theories about the NSA and/or NIST are a dime a dozen these days. And, ever since the Snowden disclosures in 2013, I am politically primed to directionally agree with distrusting the US government wholesale.

But most of the technical arguments baked into folks’ conspiracy theories make no goddamn sense .

This distrust is not exclusive to only the US government.

The goal of this blog post is not to convince you that you should trust any government; just that they are not magical or omniscient.

To that end, I’m going to explore some of the history of NSA, NIST, and cryptography standardization. Then, to explore some of the conspiracy theories that were being floated about such activity, and what we’ve learned in the years since (especially in the past month). Finally, I’m going to examine some of the current conspiracy theories floating around message boards and social media today, and explain why they’re almost certainly wrong.

Buckle up, this is going to be a tedious one.

If you find yourself asking a question like this, the correct answer is simply, “You shouldn’t.”

After all, I have never held (let alone even applied for) a security clearance, and have no access to any non-public information. I’m also not a current or former government employee, and have no aspirations to ever become one. I have access to all the same facts anyone else does.

In balance, I have no horse in the race of who trusts whom. I’m just tired of hearing the same poorly reasoned arguments all the damn time, and would like to stop having to repeat myself when I encounter one.

The sources for this, by the way, are the declassified United States Senate Select Committee on Intelligence and United States Cryptologic History .

The Data Encryption Standard (DES) was published in the Federal Register in 1975 and then standardized in 1977.

We consider it weak these days, but DES was a real game-changer for its time: It offered a standard block cipher to use for sensitive (but not classified) commercial applications. Prior to DES, the history of cryptography was largely about military uses (except a few quirky mathematicians here and there), going back before Caesar’s cipher .

From declassified documents, we now know the full story, but from the time that DES was first standardized, up until recent years, there have been a concerns about NSA’s involvement .

We sent the S-boxes off to Washington. They came back and were all different.

Alan Konheim, quoted in Applied Cryptography , p. 280

To say that academics did not trust DES would be putting it mildly: Martin Hellman (who, with Whitfield Diffie and Ralph Merkle, invented public-key cryptography) sent a letter in 1975 to the National Bureau of Standards that stated:

Whit Diffie and I have become concerned that the proposed data encryption standard, while probably secure against commercial assault, may be extremely vulnerable to attack by an intelligence organization.

Martin Hellman, re-published in this paper in 1990.

At the heart of the concern about DES was something called an S-box, which simply maps an input to an output, but whose purpose is to provide a non-linear transformation to obscure the relationship between the ciphertext and the key.

The S-box used by DES was chosen by NSA. This led a lot of people to suspect there was a backdoor in the selection of the S-boxes for DES. items.title: Truth Social Stock Crashes to All-Time Low After MAGA’s Massive Defeat: Just when you thought it couldn't sink any lower.
items.content:
Mason Lawrence / Shutterstock / Futurism

President Donald Trump spent Tuesday evening in disbelief as the walls of his carefully crafted alternate reality came crashing down around him.

On his social media echo chamber Truth Social, Trump took cheap shots at senators in his party who suffered humiliating defeats in Republican strongholds, lashed out at his allies at Fox News — going as far as to text one of its hosts in fury — and even vowed to become a “political pundit.”

Meanwhile, as he watched his personal picks fall one by one, what was left of his deserted social media platform crumbled to dust. Shares of Truth Social’s parent company, Trump Media & Technology Group (TMTG), crashed to an all-time low of just $5.23 Wednesday morning, after already spending much of the year circling the drain . After the initial publication of this story, they continued to slide, hitting another record low of just $5.06 — for a stomach-churning 61 percent lurch downward since the beginning of this year.

It’s yet another massive defeat for a company that has struggled to justify its own existence, let alone convince investors of pivots that have yet to pay off in any meaningful way. The company has attempted to reinvent itself several times, from major investments in Bitcoin and an attempted embrace prediction markets to an eyebrow-raising merger with a nuclear fusion company last year.

None of those efforts have shown any sign of life. And it’s core business is failing as well: recent analytics suggest that daily traffic on Truth Social has cratered by over 30 percent over the past year, compounding enormous losses quarter after quarter. It’s financial situation is a disaster as well, with the company reporting a staggering $238 million loss in the second quarter of this year — while earning less than $2 million over the same period.

Trump’s staggering loss in the midterms — an outcome widely seen as a major rebuke to him personally, despite not being on the ballot — is unlikely to save the company from its growing irrelevancy.

For now, the president will have to lick his wounds by complaining to the few MAGA stalwarts left on Truth Social — a sad predicament for a man who handily defeated his presidential opponent a mere two years ago.

Day 4 - Installing software, exploring the file structure

As a sysadmin, one of your key tasks is to install new software as required. You’ll also need to be very familiar with the layout of the standard directories in a Linux system.

You’ll be getting practice in both of these areas in today’s session.

Install a new application from the online repositories

Become familiar with some of the standard directories

Look at the format and content of some configuration files.

If you’ve used a smartphone “app store ” or “market”, then you’ll immediately understand the normal installation of Linux software from the standard repositories. As long as we know what the name or description of a package (=app) is, then we can search for it:

This will show a range of matching “packages”, and we can then install them with apt install command. So to install package mc (Midnight Commander) on Ubuntu:

(Unless you’re already logged in as the root user you need to use sudo before the installation commands - because an ordinary user is not permitted to install software that could impact a whole server).

Now that you have mc installed, start it by simply typing mc and pressing Enter .

This isn’t a “classic” Unix application, but once you get over the retro interface you should find navigation fairly easy, so go looking for these directories:

…and use the links in the Resources section below to begin to understand how these are used. You can also read the official manual on this hierarchy by typing man hier .

Most key configuration files are kept under /etc and subdirectories of that. These files, and the logs under /var/log are almost invariably simple text files. In the coming days you’ll be spending a lot of time with these - but for now simply use F3 to look into their contents.

Some interesting files to look at are: /etc/passwd , /etc/ssh/sshd_config and /var/log/auth.log

Use F3 again to exit from viewing a file.

F10 will exit mc , although you may need to use your mouse to select it.

(On an Apple Mac in Terminal, you may need to use ESC+3 to get F3 and ESC+0 for F10)

Now use apt search to search for and install some more packages: Try searching for “hangman”. You will probably find that an old text-based version is included in a package called bsdgames . Install and play a couple of rounds…

Post your progress, comments and questions to the forum.

Use mc to view /etc/apt/sources.list.d/ubuntu.sources where the actual locations of the repositories are specified. Often these will be “mirror” sites that are closer to your server than the main Ubuntu servers.

Read Repositories - CommandLine for more of the gory details.

items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

제가 집에서 한 말이나 제 언니랑 한 말들을 학교 가면 다 알고있어요 그래서 제가 말한 내용이랑 똑같은 내용을 꼭 제가 들을 수 있을때 언급하고 남자애들 여자애들 할것없이 제가 안보이는 데에서 조금만 이상한 말 하면 비웃으면서 지나가요 ㅠ 제가 진짜 친구가 없어서 학교에서 한마디도 안하는 날들이 대부분인데 제가 언니랑 학교 구석에서 말한 내용이랑 집에서 혼잣말 한 내용들을 똑같이 언급한게 한두번이 아니에요 ㅠ 제가 그냥 내용만 겹치면 말을 않겠는데 제가 말했던 내용 언급하면서 꼭 제 이름도 한번씩 부르고 그래요 보통 사람들은 자기이름을 그렇게 말하면 기분나빠서 한번 돌아보기라도 하겠지만 저는 성격이 워낙 내성적이라 누가 비웃고 지나가거나 째려보거나 저 보면서 한숨쉬어도 아무말도 못하거든요 ㅠ 그래서 그냥 기분만 나쁜건데 이게 하루이틀 쌓이니까 너무 힘들더라고요 ㅠ 처음엔 저도 이게 정신이 약간 아픈건가 했는데 정신병 관련 영상도 다 보고 그랬는데 환청은 이런식으로 들리는게 아니라고 하더라고요 계속 날 비난하고 그런식으로 들리는건데 저는 그런게 전혀 아니라 제가 전날 했던 얘기들, 방금 쉬는시간에 학교 구석에서 나눈 얘기들을 자꾸 똑같이 언급하니까 미치겠어요 ㅠ 한두번 우연으로 겹치는게 아니라 계속 겹쳐요 진짜.. 그리고 애초에 제가 학교에서 말을 한마디도 안하는데 자꾸 저한테 그런 반응을 보인다는게 애초에 저한테 이상한 일이 일어난다는 반증 아닌가요? 그리고 걔네가 말했던걸 몇개를 말씀드려보면 제가 도청을 의심한 초기에 급식실에서 밥먹고있었는데 어떤 남자애가 “도청” 이러고 지나가는거에요 그리고 저희반 남자애가 제 언니 이동수업반이랑 같은 반인데 거기서 쉬는시간에 “도청기를 달고다녀 ㅋㅋㅋㅋ” 이랬다는거에요 진짜 이상하죠 저는 예전에 우울증 약을 먹은적이 있어서 정신이 막 무결점으로 건강한 편은 아니에요 근데 저희 언니는 그런적도 없고 교우관계도 좋고 진짜 정신이 건강하거든요 ㅠ 근데 저희 언니가 그런말을 들었다니깐 진짜 도청이 일어나는게 맞는거구나 생각했어요.. 그리고 또 있었던 일을 말씀드리면 이동수업 때 제 뒷쪽에서 남자애가 제 아버지 직업을 언급하면서 제 이름을 말하는거에요 이게 도청을 하지 않고서는 절대 알수가 없는 사실이거든요 ㅠ 또 “정신병ㅋㅋㅋ” 하면서 제 이름을 언급하는거에요 이것도 도청을 하지 않았다면 알수 없는거고요 더 말씀드릴 사례가 많은데 그러면 너무 길어져서 이정도만 말씀드릴게요 그래서 찾아보니까 머리에 붙일수 있는 초소형 도청기가 있다길래  제 언니가 제 머리를 샅샅이 뒤져줬거든요? 근데 그래도 아무것도 안나오더라고요 ㅠ 그리고 또 도청 탐지 업체를 알아보니까 금액이 너무 비싸서요 ㅠ 제가 고3인데 이런일을 당해서 너무 스트레스 받는데 방법이 없어서 정말 어떻게 해야될지 모르겠어요 안그래도 제가 여자애들이나 남자애들이 괴롭힐 소재가 많은 조용한 애거든요 ㅠ그래서 저를 지나칠때 꼭 한마디 끼얹고 지나가고 그래서 학교생활이 막 편한 그런애는 아닌데 학교에서 유일하게 맘놓고 말할 수 있는 언니랑 말하는 얘기를 다 알고있으니까 스트레스 받아서 공부 능력도 점점 떨어지는것같고 쨋든 걱정이 이만저만이 아니에요 어떡해야되죠 ㅠㅠ 제가 성격이 활발한 편도 아니고 집에 돈이 많지도 않아서 진짜 대학 잘가야되는데 걱정이에요ㅠㅠ 긴글 읽어주셔서 감사하고요 여기가 사생활 침해 관련한 갤러리니까 혹여나 저랑 비슷한 경험이 있으시거나 관련 지식이 있는 분은 제가 어떻게 해야하는건지 알려주시면 진짜진짜 감사드릴것같아요 많은 도움 부탁드려요 정말 방법 여러가지 찾아봐도 안되겠어서 여기다 글 남겨요

items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-62662 📢 Source: GitHub_M 💣 CVSS Score: 0.0 (NA) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: False Pocket ID is an OIDC provider that allows users to authenticate with their passkeys to services. From 1.11.0 until 2.10.0, createTokenFromClientCredentials in backend/internal/service/oidc_service.go accepts the client-controlled resource parameter and embeds it directly in the access token aud claim without validating that the audience is registered or that the requesting client may access it. Any authenticated OIDC client can therefore obtain a Pocket ID-signed token naming another client or an arbitrary audience. The /api/oidc/introspect endpoint cannot distinguish the unauthorized token because it treats a token as active when the introspecting client's identifier matches the attacker-selected audience. In deployments where resource servers trust Pocket ID access tokens for service-to-service authorization, this bypasses audience-based access controls and can permit unauthorized data access or actions; deployments that do not use these tokens for resource-server authorization have no immediate exploitable impact. This issue is fixed in version 2.10.0. 📅 Published Date: 2026-11-04T22:29:36.917Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-62662
items.title_ko: CVE-2026-62662: Pocket ID의 토큰 audience 검증 누락
items.summary_ko: Pocket ID 1.11.0부터 2.10.0까지 createTokenFromClientCredentials 함수는 클라이언트가 지정한 resource 파라미터를 검증 없이 access token의 aud 클레임에 넣는다. 이로써 인증된 OIDC 클라이언트가 다른 클라이언트나 임의 대상을 지정한 토큰을 받을 수 있다. 리소스 서버가 이 토큰을 서비스 간 인가에 신뢰하는 환경에서는 접근 통제가 우회될 수 있으며, 2.10.0에서 수정됐다.
items.content_ko: Pocket ID는 사용자가 패스키로 서비스에 인증하도록 돕는 OIDC 제공자다. 1.11.0부터 2.10.0까지 backend/internal/service/oidc_service.go의 createTokenFromClientCredentials 함수는 클라이언트가 보낸 resource 파라미터를 검증하지 않고 access token의 aud 클레임에 그대로 넣는다. 이 때문에 인증된 OIDC 클라이언트는 다른 클라이언트나 임의의 audience를 지정한 Pocket ID 서명 토큰을 얻을 수 있다. /api/oidc/introspect 엔드포인트는 내성 조사하는 클라이언트 식별자가 공격자가 지정한 audience와 일치하면 토큰을 활성 상태로 판단하므로, 이 무단 토큰을 구별하지 못한다. 리소스 서버가 액세스 토큰을 서비스 간 인가에 쓰는 배포에서는 audience 기반 접근 통제가 우회되어 무단 데이터 접근이나 작업이 허용될 수 있다. 이 토큰을 리소스 서버 인가에 쓰지 않는 배포에는 즉각적인 악용 영향이 없다고 설명된다. 수정 버전은 2.10.0이다.

items.title: North Korean fake job interview led to $6.3B Binance heist
items.content:
North Korean fake job interview led to $6.3B Binance heist

'It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident,' exchange says

FBI pins $6.3B Binance crypto heist on North Korean hackers

Google says Asian advertisers spending less due to Europe's customs changes

In the year AI re-wrote the infosec rulebook, it’s comforting to know crypto exchanges still have bad security

Attackers turn GitHub issues into supply chain campaign against 61 public repos in less than an hour

China's spaceplane bears striking resemblance to America's X-37B

North Korean cryptocurrency thieves tricked a Binance software engineer into downloading malware onto their work-issued computer during a fake job interview process before last week's record-breaking $6.3 billion heist .

In an incident report published on Tuesday, the cryptocurrency exchange said several techniques - including social engineering via fake job interviews, malware downloads, compromised internal AI tooling, endpoint takeover, and an “advanced transaction-authorization method” - led to the October 29 security breach.

“Our current investigation indicates that this was a sophisticated, multi-stage campaign,” the incident report said. “It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident.”

Over the weekend, the FBI attributed the theft to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking operation linked to Lazarus Group , known for combining espionage with massive cryptocurrency heists . The Pyongyang-backed crew is also highly adept at job market scams - both posing as IT workers , who are then hired by Western companies , and as potential employers to lure software engineers into downloading malware and infecting corporate devices .

With the recent Binance attack, the Norks used the latter.

The attack prep began back in June with a supply chain attack when one of its engineers downloaded a malicious Homebrew installation . While the malware was detected by the security team, the device was replaced, and all affected credentials rotated, “Engineer A’s role and his related colleagues on our wallet infrastructure team was exposed to the hacker,” the report says.

Three months later, the social engineering part of the attack happened.

In September, another software engineer was contacted via a “legitimate job-hunting platform” by someone purporting to be a project director who arranged a series of job interviews for the Binance engineer with the fake company. During the first round - a live video interview with the engineer and a fake HR rep - the interviewer “shared a social media account with him, including personal photos and videos posted on the platform, in order to build trust,” according to the report. “This was more advanced and deceptive than previously seen social engineering approaches.”

The second interview with someone purporting to be the CEO of the phony company was conducted on a “popular social chat app,” and toward the end, the CEO instructed the engineer to download an “assignment” containing a malware-laced code repository. The code executed on his work computer during the setup process, which kicked off a series of unauthorized activities.

According to Binance, the malware replaced a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version, which executed commands and established communication with an attacker-controlled external server. The attackers also took steps to hide the malicious script and evade detection, and it worked. Binance’s endpoint security tools did not immediately detect the malware.

CREATE  /opt/homebrew/Cellar/pyenv/2.8.0/libexec/pyenv_

DELETE  .../libexec/pyenv  (3,344 B)      ← remove the valid pyenv

RENAME  pyenv_ → pyenv  (3,414 B)  ← replace it with a malicious version

DELETE  /opt/homebrew/bin/pyenv  (3,414 B)

ln  (create a new symlink)  +  spawn zsh

Then, on October 20, the miscreants used the compromised computer and an internal AI tool to gain access to the computers of wallet DevOps engineer A…

items.title: Introducing Adaptive Dark Mode
items.summary: css, web
items.content:
by Simon Fraser, Luming Yin, Lily Spiniolas, Joanne Pan, Veda Periwal and Jen Simmons

We’re excited to announce Adaptive Dark Mode in Safari 27.3 beta. When enabled by a user, Safari adapts light websites and presents them as dark.

In the spring of 2019, Safari 12.1 became the first browser to support dark mode on the web. A lot of people love using dark mode, but not every website has a dark version. Almost 40% of web page loads are from users in dark mode, and yet only 10% of page loads support it. If you love dark mode, you’ve probably hit a site that felt particularly bright . Adaptive Dark Mode is designed to close that gap, providing a consistent dark experience across the web.

You can try it today in Safari 27.3 beta. To enable, first make sure your system appearance is set to dark. Then browse to a website with a bright background. Safari will offer a preview of Adaptive Dark Mode. Tap ‘Try’.

For websites that signal support of dark mode with <meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark"> in HTML or color-scheme: light dark in CSS, Adaptive Dark Mode does not change a thing. For the rest of the web, it quickly analyzes the page, looking at colors and estimating whether it’s predominantly light or dark. If the page generally has a dark background with light text, nothing is changed. When a page has a light appearance, Adaptive Dark Mode adapts the page to be dark.

At the core of Adaptive Dark Mode is the transformation of color. Sometimes colors are simply decorative, while other times they have semantic meaning. Adaptive Dark Mode determines when to invert colors so elements remain visible or when to leave colors unchanged.

While creating Adaptive Dark Mode, we developed a color matrix to invert the luminosity of colors while preserving hue. It’s used to make light backgrounds dark, and dark text light. When transforming text color, Adaptive Dark Mode aims for sufficient contrast as defined by the WCAG 4.5:1 contrast ratio . Light CSS gradients are also transformed to dark.

Adaptive Dark Mode makes careful judgments so transformed content looks good and stays usable: buttons have contrast against backgrounds, text is visible over images, and hover menus look clear.

It takes the same care with images. Most are left unchanged, preserving their integrity. But many icons and logos can lose contrast when the background color behind them is inverted. So Adaptive Dark Mode inspects SVG images and transforms colors when needed. For bitmap images, it analyzes the pixel histograms and inverts simple black-and-white logos.

Effects like masks and mix-blend-mode can create undesirable results on an element whose colors have been transformed, so in some cases Adaptive Dark Mode turns such effects off. Also, <canvas> content is left unchanged, since canvases contain a wide range of content that’s hard to predict.

It’s precisely because Adaptive Dark Mode is happening deep within the WebKit browser engine that we are able to find creative ways to solve the most complex challenges, apply the transformations with great speed and power efficiency, all while rigorously protecting user privacy.

In general, a web page will work well with Adaptive Dark Mode if it follows good modern web development practices.

If your site still uses older techniques, small updates can help. For logos and icons, swap bitmap images for SVG. Use solid or gradient colors in CSS instead of tiled background images. Replace image sprites with modern CSS for rounded corners, shadows, and button states. Create content images with transparent backgrounds instead of baking the page background color into the image. Add padding to containers to prevent crowding.

Perhaps you want a specific dark mode experience for a certain portion of the page. Apply color-scheme: light dark to the relevant element and add your own dark styles.

For complete control over how your site looks in dark mode, add full support. It’s a terrific time to do so. It’s never been…

items.title: Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs
items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

Weak security means attackers could disable all of a city's public EV chargers

US regulator tells GM to hit the brakes on customer tracking

21K Nissan customers' data stolen in Red Hat raid

Porsche panic in Russia as pricey status symbols forget how to car

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

The carmaker didn't respond to questions about how many current and former employees are affected, when Oracle first notified it of the breach, and whether the compromise was limited to Oracle-managed systems. ®

items.title: The Tech Industry Went All in on Trump, and Now They’re in Serious Danger Now That Americans Have Turned on Him: They gambled... and lost.
items.content:
Tech companies threw their lot in with Donald Trump, and now, following a blue tsunami, they’re poised to pay the price. If it wasn’t already clear before the first vote was cast, it’s now undeniable that these midterm elections were in no small part a referendum on Big Tech.

A preponderance of Democratic candidates for congress, the senate, and state governorship supported some form of data center moratorium. Across ten states, Ballotpedia showed , over 40 ballot measures were put forth related to regulating data centers. A full 56 percent of Americans considered AI and data centers a crucial or major factor in their votes, according to NBC News exit polls . Many of the Democratic challengers, including senator-elect Sherrod Brown in Ohio, flipped seats while raging against data center construction.

“What we just witnessed was an AI earthquake,” Brad Carson, co-founder of Americans for Responsible Innovation, told Axios . “Voters just sent a clear message that they want rules for AI and data centers.”

Greg Casar, a Texas Democratic congressman who just secured reelection, echoed this analogy, calling the election an “early tremor of a much bigger AI earthquake upending American politics.”

One of the biggest setbacks to the tech industry is Gina Hinojosa’s victory in the Texas governor race, defeating Republican incumbent Greg Abott. Texas is where many AI companies are banking building their data center empires, holding an overwhelming 27 percent of the entire country’s planned data center capacity, according to widely-cited Wells Fargo data . Many tech figures have spent the past few years relocating operations there, including former trillionaire Elon Musk.

“The entire AI industry made this giant levered bet on the idea that they’d be able to build [data centers] in Texas,” Sam Koppelman at Hunterbrook Media, an investigative journalism outlet, told Politico . “This election totally changed that.”

Analysts at SemiAnalysis ahead of the election feared the worst, believing Hinojosa would come down hard on the industry: “she would impose a moratorium until legislation is passed that gives communities a voice, protects household utility bills, and ends the tax incentives for data centers,” the firm wrote, per Bloomberg reporting .

Along with Texas, Democratic governor candidates prevailing in George and Michigan now means that the hammer could be brought down on 45 percent of planned US data center capacity.

Musk encapsulated the palpable sense of dread over this new reality in a post-elections tweet : “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”

Dan Ives, a partner at the bank Yorkville Ives & Co, was more direct. “There is no way to sugarcoat that Democrats taking control especially over the Senate will create some major hurdles for AI and tech legislation in the Beltway over the next 2 years,” he said in a note, quoted by CNBC .

Beyond the issue of data centers themselves, Republican candidates lost because they reeked of big tech money. Elon Musk poured $474 million into the midterms, including $224 million in Texas alone. OpenAI president Greg Brockman, and Silicon Valley VC heavyweights Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz, splurged on a super PAC for pro-AI candidates, most of them Republicans. And yet, a Guardrails Action survey before the election found that three quarters of likely voters in Iowa, Michigan, and Ohio — where blue candidates for the senate and governorship all prevailed — said that they would be less apt to vote for a candidate if they found out they had accepted a donation from an AI Super PAC.

Also leaving a lasting impression on voters is how Big Tech has constantly appeased president Trump and complied with even his most arbitrary whims. Trump demanded that the term “artificial intelligence” be rebranded as “Super Intelligence,” and AI companies, with a straight face, started using it in their communications. items.title: Making features generic in CSS
items.content:
CSS has two new positional alignment keywords as part of CSS Box Alignment Level 3 : flow-start and flow-end . These are defined as aliases for the existing flex-start and flex-end keywords. Therefore, in a supporting browser, the following two lines should align flex items to the end of the flex container (the right assuming you are working in English).

You can read the discussion that led to this change in the issue on Github , including the IRC transcript of the meeting where the resolution was made. Making this change means these keywords can also be used in grid lanes (masonry) layout.

This is not the first time the CSS Working Group has taken a property or value name that was tied to a particular layout method and generalised it. The gap properties for grid and flexbox started life as grid-gap properties. Use grid-gap rather than gap in your code, and you will still get a gap between grid tracks. If developers have started to use the property or value by the change is made, it will live forever as an alias, to prevent us from breaking the web .

You might wonder why these properties and values were designed to be specific to one layout method. Perhaps the Working Group could have foreseen that there might be new layout methods requiring the same type of flow end as flexbox, or gaps as in grid—we do have a list of things we’re intending to fix once time travel is invented . However, it’s sometimes useful to scope things down to one layout method, and it’s not always easy to see into the future to decide which things that applies to.

I’ve just returned from W3C TPAC in Dublin and two days of CSS Working Group meetings where a couple of things in this category were discussed.

The CSS reading-flow property controls the order that items in grid, flex, and block layouts are exposed in terms of focus order. It lets you manage the issue where a grid layout can move items around so they are tabbed to in an unintuitive way. The new grid lanes layout mode can create this kind of disconnect and, as the final layout is not controlled by the web developer, without reading-flow support there’s no way to control that experience. We have already resolved to add support, at the meeting at TPAC we needed to resolve on the names of the grid lanes properties . The final resolution was to use grid-lanes-flow and grid-lanes-track , specific values for grid lanes.

Why do we have specific values for the reading-flow property for each type of layout? Partly this is because the layout methods have different needs, only grid layout has both columns and rows, for example. Having common values would mean that in some layout methods only some of the values would do anything, which is confusing. In addition, because the reading-flow property messes with focus order, we wanted to make sure that when people used it, they were very carefully doing so, with consideration of the specific thing they were trying to achieve. I don’t expect most grid layouts to need this property, as the source order is very likely to be the best focus order. By adding the friction of needing to use the right values for the layout, we prevent a global switching on of a ‘visual’ flow.

There has been a long discussion about implementing masonry in CSS, with different proposals from the Webkit and Chrome teams. A key decision that had to be made was whether masonry was to be part of CSS Grid Layout, or its own value of display . I’ve held the view, even before I was part of the Chrome team, that it should be a separate thing. The main reason for this is detailed in this blog post on developer.chrome.com . Masonry is a very specific type of layout, and by including it in grid, we have to allow lot of complex grid things to also work in masonry. This includes things that already exist, and also anything we add to grid in the future. Similar to the values of reading-flow , sometimes things are just different enough that it’s best to keep them separate so that they aren’t…

items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

items.title: AMD expects to outsell Intel in Q4 for the first time in history
items.content:
AMD late on Tuesday reported its highest quarterly revenue ever as demand for its Epyc data center processors and Instinct AI accelerators nearly doubled year-over year and sales of its products for client systems were down only modestly despite high memory prices and other headwinds.

As increasing sales of data center hardware more than offset declines in the client realms, AMD's profitability continues to improve. Perhaps the most striking announcement AMD made is that it expects its Q4 revenue to reach approximately $17 billion, which would put it ahead of Intel for the first time in history.

AMD's third-quarter revenue reached $13.377 billion, a huge increase from $9.25 billion in the same quarter a year earlier and $11.54 billion in the previous quarter. The company's gross margin was 54% during the quarter, and net income increased by 95% to $2.43 billion. Diluted earnings per share reached $1.46, compared with $0.75 in the same quarter last year.

Data center business now accounts for 64% of AMD's revenue

AMD's Data Center business was the main driver of its growth as the unit's sales reached a record $8.55 billion, up 97% from $4.34 billion a year earlier and 27% sequentially. The unit's operating income surged by 168% to $2.88 billion, while operating margin expanded from 25% to 34%.

(Image credit: AMD) The company attributed the results to strong demand for its latest Epyc processors and the launch of Instinct MI455X AI accelerators, which power its Helios rack-scale systems. Specifically, AMD noted that Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft , OpenAI, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure are already running workloads on their first Helios systems.

AMD expects its Data Center revenue to increase from $8.55 billion in Q3 2026 to approximately $12.8 billion in Q4 (based on the company's guidance), driven by the ramp of Instinct MI455X accelerators and Helios systems. The company also projects that its server CPU revenue will double in 2027, while Data Center AI accelerator and rack revenue will more than double, which will push the DC unit's contribution to over 80% of total company sales, up from 64% this past quarter and from 47% in Q3 2025.

"We now expect server revenue to double year over year in 2027 and data center AI revenue to grow even faster than we projected ninety days ago," said Lisa Su, chief executive and chairman of AMD, during the company's earnings call with analysts and investors. "As a result, we expect data center to be more than eighty percent of our total revenue in 2027 and to drive the majority of our revenue and earnings growth."

AMD's Client and Gaming business unit generated $3.722 billion in revenue, down 8% year-over-year and 3% quarter-over-quarter.

(Image credit: AMD) Meanwhile, sales of AMD's client CPUs totaled $2.95 billion, down from $3.06 billion in the previous quarter and up around $200 million from $2.75 billion in the same quarter a year ago.

Sales of AMD's gaming products — including discrete GPUs and system-on-chips for game consoles — dropped to $773 million from $1.298 billion in the previous year as Microsoft and Sony bought fewer console SoCs, while sales of discrete Radeon RX GPUs remained weak during the quarter. The combined segment's operating income dropped by 34% to $573 million as the unit's operating margin decreased to 15%.

"In 2027, we are planning for PC market unit shipments to decline by a double-digit percentage," Su said. "In this environment, we expect to outperform the market as we deliver our rising roadmap and grow our commercial footprint."

items.title: C++26 Disapproved
items.content:
On October 23, 2026, the unthinkable happened. It was supposed to be a mere formality: C++26 was up for a vote by the ISO National Bodies (NBs). The options are always approval, rejection, or abstention. Comments are also allowed. Since 1998, this process had run quietly and smoothly. Not so on October 23, 2026. After a twelve-week voting period, the result is in: Disapproved !

I would like to mention here that I am a member of the C++ Standardization Committee and, together with my colleagues, represent Germany’s vote. ISO rules also stipulate that certain votes are internal to ISO, and the results—or the breakdown of the results—may not be published. This article contains my own personal views.

As far as I know, this is the first time in the history of C++ that DIS ballot failed. When I searched the ISO system, I could only find one other DIS that was not approved: ISO/IEC DIS 26926 C++/CLI Language Specification dated August 11, 2006. It’s possible that my search privileges aren’t sufficient to view everything, but all ISO programming languages should be visible to me. The sad end of ISO/IEC DIS 26926: the project was halted. I mention this upfront to clarify the significance of this vote.

In the following, I will use various terms from everyday ISO terminology. At https://isocpp.org/std/iso-iec-jtc1-procedures , there is an overview of the various stages of an ISO standard. DIS is the penultimate stage. As the overview also shows, a two-thirds majority is required. This majority was not achieved.

The reason for the rejection is quite clear from the comments submitted by the National Bodies (NBs): contracts. Put simply, a number of NBs believe that this feature is not yet ready for release.

Now it gets complicated. The C++ Standardization Committee, also known as WG21, follows ISO rules but also has some additional rules. One of these is (or was) that opinions are always heard whenever new information becomes available. If an opinion was heard and a feature was nevertheless not changed as desired, the person respects the outcome and accepts that many others disagree.

However, the voting body at the NB level may also consist of other individuals, or the NBs are, of course, free to vote differently.

The previous practice was that NBs would only vote against a standard if new information became available or if errors in the process or similar issues were identified. This changed on October 23, 2026.

It’s difficult to judge in this complex situation; the NBs who want C++26 without Contracts argue that there is new information. I myself find it hard to share this view. A new paper with old arguments is not new information to me.

The feature has been on the wish list for a long time. I was already in the room in Cologne back in 2019, at the time for C++20, when Contracts, in a different form back then, were being included in the standard. I was also in the room when the feature was removed from C++20 again during the same meeting. As a result, a study group was formed to address the topic of Contracts and its various aspects from 2020 to approximately 2024. Afterward, the study group submitted its work and proposals to the Evolution Working Group (EWG), the central body for language extensions. There, the topic was discussed further over several meetings before being included in C++26 by a majority vote.

In the next step, WG21 voted on the C++26 draft in March 2026, which included Contracts. Here, too, a large majority was achieved, though not without dissenting votes.

And that brings us to the next phase: DIS. At this stage, there were enough “no” votes that a two-thirds majority was not reached.

items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. One term stood out for its specificity, chikungunya , the mosquito-borne virus behind a 2025 outbreak in China's Guangdong province.

Start with REDCap. Patch externally facing servers and remove old versions outright, not just alongside the current build. REDCap lets legacy versions run side-by-side, and that is what enables downgrade attacks, where an attacker forces software back to a known-vulnerable release.

Then check the mail side. Review Workspace, or equivalent, content compliance and mail-forwarding rules for anything that BCCs or reroutes mail to outside addresses. Check admin audit logs for when rules changed, not just what they say now. Pull GTIG's published indicators and hunt for INFINITERED. items.title: Elon Musk in Real Trouble After Humiliating Defeat: "Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time."
items.content:
In late 2020, after months of forcing employees back to the assembly line in the midst of a growing pandemic, Elon Musk decided he’d had enough of being held accountable by regulators in California — and moved to Texas .

“California has been winning for a long time, and I think they’re taking it for granted,” Musk said at the time. “Silicon Valley has too much influence in the world.”

The move, largely seen as a way to avoid regulatory hurdles, environmental laws, and progressive taxation, culminated in Musk moving the headquarters of both Tesla and SpaceX to the Lone Star state. South Texas is now home to SpaceX’s so-called “Starbase,” a massive and growing rocket development campus that has run run foul of both locals and federal regulators alike.

But now, after a historic landslide victory for Democrats this week, Musk’s decision to go all-in on Texas — not to mention the whopping $474 million he spent on supporting Republican nominees nationwide — is looking like a drastic misfire. Democrats swept Texas , with voters picking James Talarico as senator, Gina Hinojosa as governor, and Nathan Johnson as attorney general.

The stock market immediately punished Musk for the humiliating defeat, with shares of both Tesla and Texas plummeting as soon as the market opened on Wednesday.

The election results could also throw a major wrench in Musk’s sizable AI investments and data center construction efforts. One of the biggest winners of late Tuesday’s victory were opponents of data center development, setting the stage for more moratoriums. In fact, Hinojosa has already called for one, as well as an end to tax breaks for the industry.

While it’s a win for countless Americans who have opposed the facilities, billionaires like Musk could be faced with a major headache.

“There is no way to sugarcoat that Democrats taking control especially over the Senate will create some major hurdles for AI and tech legislation in the Beltway over the next two years,” Musk loyalist and tech analyst Dan Ives said in a note on Wednesday morning .

A sulking Musk is already looking to move on from the humiliation, actively distancing himself from the major data center push.

“Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” he tweeted after many hours of uncharacteristic silence, referring to SpaceX’s plans to develop orbital data centers.

“Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time,” he added in a separate post .

As much as he might joke, the richest people in the world could soon be held accountable.

“We must get big money out of our politics, so no billionaire or trillionaire can buy our elections,” Talarico said during his victory speech.

items.title: 글 쌌다 지웠다 하는 뷩쉰은 봐라
items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

개별 이미지들의 위치 변경, 삭제, 별칭 추가, 폴더명 변경을 할 수 있습니다
