items.title: HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

“Attackers no longer need massive datasets to make use of synthetic speech tooling,” Douglas McKee, Rapid7’s director of vulnerability intelligence, said in a blog post . “In many cases, they just need clean source audio of the right person saying enough words in enough contexts. That has made executive voice data, call recordings, and live conversation capture far more valuable than many organizations seem prepared…

items.title: British fintech Revolut slashes AI coding costs 10x by cutting out Claude and going self-hosted
items.content:
British fintech Revolut slashes AI coding costs 10x by cutting out Claude and going self-hosted

Turns out cheap tokens get engineers doing things that save time, like debugging and tackling Jira tickets

Datacenter operators must win hearts and minds, not just permits

AMD on track to overtake Intel as biggest x86 outfit

Nvidia is happy to take your money whether you're using open or closed models, says Jensen Huang

Drax wants to feed Britain's AI habit with £20B datacenter at biomass power station

Toyota shows off SoC that stores model weights and its OS on integrated memory

Revolut says that in less than a year it's managed to slash its AI coding inference costs by roughly 90 percent by making self-hosted models its default instead of relying primarily on commercial services like Claude.

Speaking at the AI Engineer conference in New York last month, David Abitbol, ops and infrastructure lead at the British fintech, described how it saw a 60 percent improvement in coding time and a 70 percent improvement in lead time following its rollout of AI coding tools to roughly 2,000 engineers. Revolut initially adopted GLM-5.1 before moving to GLM-5.3, which it now serves using 56 Nvidia B200 GPUs.

Prior to its switch to GLM, Revolut had been experimenting with AI, deploying Gemini in early 2025 and Claude Code in early 2026. "We were highly skeptical about the cost of AI. We were seeing engineers spend $1,000 a month, $10,000 a month with not so much ROI, and so when we launched it we launched it with strict budget limits," Abitbol said.

Because of this, engineers only had access to a limited number of tokens, so the company began investigating self-hosting its own models. At $0.30 per million input/output tokens, self hosting GLM 5.1 cost about a tenth of using OpenAI's Codex or Anthropic's Claude Code. And, as it turned out, when tokens are cheap, you stop worrying about how many they use or what they use them for.

While Revolut did see improvements to coding speed, Abitbol noted the biggest bottleneck wasn't actually the code. Instead, he says the biggest gains came from letting the AI models deal with things like debugging and Jira and Confluence tickets. "When you have unlimited tokens, you're free to do that," he said. "You no longer have to save your tokens for the end of the quarter or the most difficult task."

Developed by Chinese open weights model dev Z.ai, GLM 5.1 isn't exactly a small model. At roughly 754 billion total parameters (40 billion activated for each token generated), the model requires roughly 380 GB of GPU memory just to hold the weights and another 6-26 GB per user to maintain context depending on precision.

To serve GLM-5.3 at scale, Revolut deployed 56 Nvidia B200 GPUs, equivalent in GPU count to seven eight-GPU DGX B200 systems. But as Abitbol noted, the greatest performance gains didn't come from adding GPUs, but rather tuning the model's hyperparameters along with switching to NVFP4 quantization, implementing disaggregated prefill and decode, and tuning context lengths.

One key takeaway was that supporting a one-million-token context window doesn't necessarily make such a large window useful or efficient. "Long context is a scam. You really need to be mindful of that," Abitbol said. "Even though you can serve one million tokens, 256 [thousand] is really what you need."

With these optimizations, Abitbol says that the company was able to achieve sub 3-second time to first token on context windows of around 256,000 tokens, and generation speeds of around 200 tokens a second, both of which he notes are the sweet spot for the company's software engineers.

"What you want to aim for is a sub-3 second time to first token. This is empirical evidence. As soon as you exceed 5 seconds, my Slack inbox starts to blow up," Abitbol said. "In terms of throughput, it doesn't really matter as much. We serve, in terms of interactivity, 200 tokens per second. People are fine [with that]. You don't need to go…

items.title: A new Go API for JSON
items.summary: go
items.content:
Michael Pratt, Joe Tsai, Daniel Martí, Johan Brandhorst-Satzkorn, Roger Peppe, Chris Hines, and Damien Neil

JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) is a simple data interchange format, the most popular data format used on the internet, and widely read and written by Go programs.

Go has included support for JSON in the standard library since well before Go 1.0.

We first we wrote about support for JSON in Go more than 15 years ago!

Over time, packages evolve with the needs of their users, and encoding/json is no exception.

Last year, we wrote about a new experimental API for JSON designed to bring long-awaited improvements and fixes.

After additional feedback and refinement, the new encoding/json/v2 and encoding/json/jsontext packages are stable and generally available in Go 1.27!

This post is an updated version of the article introducing the experiment , describing the problems with encoding/json , and an introduction to the new packages.

Overall, encoding/json has held up well.

The idea of marshaling and unmarshaling arbitrary Go types

with some default representation in JSON, combined with the ability to

customize the representation, has proven to be highly flexible.

However, in the years since its introduction,

various users have identified numerous shortcomings.

There are various behavioral flaws in encoding/json :

Imprecise handling of JSON syntax : Over the years, JSON has seen

increased standardization in order for programs to properly communicate.

Generally, decoders have become stricter at rejecting ambiguous inputs,

to reduce the chance that two implementations will have different

(successful) interpretations of a particular JSON value.

encoding/json currently accepts invalid UTF-8,

whereas the latest Internet Standard (RFC 8259) requires valid UTF-8.

The default behavior should report an error in the presence of invalid UTF-8,

instead of introducing silent data corruption,

encoding/json currently accepts objects with duplicate member names.

RFC 8259 does not specify how to handle duplicate names,

so an implementation is free to choose an arbitrary value,

merge the values, discard the values, or report an error.

The presence of a duplicate name results in a JSON value

without a universally agreed upon meaning.

This could be exploited by attackers in security applications

and has been exploited before (as in CVE-2017-12635 ).

The default behavior should err on the side of safety and reject duplicate names.

Leaking nilness of slices and maps : JSON is often used to communicate with

programs using JSON implementations that do not allow null to be unmarshaled

into a data type expected to be a JSON array or object.

Since encoding/json marshals a nil slice or map as a JSON null ,

this may lead to errors when unmarshaling by other implementations.

indicated that most Go users prefer that nil slices and maps

items.title: Miasma Worm Targets AI Coding Agents: 73 Microsoft Azure Repos Disabled
items.content:
An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

By bypassing registries and package managers entirely, the Miasma worm targeted the very tools developers use to write code. It didn’t wait for npm install . Instead, it waited for the developer to simply open their code editor or launch an AI coding assistant.

The genius of the Miasma repository-poisoning campaign lies in its exploit surface. When an attacker successfully pushed malicious commits to targeted codebases (such as the popular library icflorescu/mantine-datatable ), the commits added no actual code dependencies.

Instead, the attacker checked in five innocent-looking workspace configuration files and one obfuscated JavaScript file: .github/setup.js .

│ └── settings . json < - - Claude Code SessionStart Hook

│ └── setup . mdc < - - Cursor Agent Prompt Injection

│ └── settings . json < - - Gemini CLI SessionStart Hook

│ └── tasks . json < - - VS Code Automatic Folder - Open Task

├── package . json < -- Hijacked NPM Test Script

└── setup . js < - - The 4.3 MB Staged Dropper

Each of these configuration files is designed to abuse a legitimate, developer-friendly auto-run feature within popular modern tools. Opening the cloned directory in any of these environments instantly triggers execution.

Claude Code & Gemini CLI (SessionStart Hooks)

Both Anthropic’s Claude Code and Google’s Gemini CLI support custom hooks triggered when an AI agent initializes a session in a project workspace. Miasma exploits this by defining a blanket wildcard matcher that forces the agent to execute the dropper via Node.js before any developer prompt is processed.

items.title: Guerrilla bike lanes: San Francisco makes illicit infrastructure permanent (2016)
items.content:
When two cyclists were tragically  killed in hit-and-run collisions this past summer, a group of anonymous urban activists known as the San Francisco Transformation Agency erected a set of protected bike lanes using traffic cones. Usually such  guerrilla interventions are temporary. They raise awareness but ultimately get taken down by municipal authorities. But when the same group recently (and illegally) installed a set of soft-hit posts alongside Golden Gate Park, the city reacted by  making the change official .

The SFMTrA , a play on the city’s Municipal Transportation Agency (SFMTA), “is a collective organization of men and women committed to making streets safer for cyclists and pedestrians, and doing it quickly.” According to the organization, their members use tactical urbanism to accomplish a range of objectives, including:

Provide a real safety increase for cyclists and pedestrians.

Draw attention to areas of the city that are unsafe for vulnerable pedestrians and cyclists.

Put pressure on the SFMTA and public officials to make proactive, rapid and substantive improvements in street safety.

Many of their interventions involve orange traffic cones , which do grab visual attention but are also impermanent and easily damaged. Adding more robust traffic delineators (also known as soft or safe hit posts) may have helped persuade the city to retain this particular recent installation along John F. Kennedy Drive.

“Generally, we have no choice but to remove cones and posts that do not go through an official process,” wrote the city agency in a statement , “because it’s a code violation to place objects in the roadway, and they could create conflicts for various types of traffic.” But in this case, they plan to install official safe hit posts and leave the temporary ones in place until their review process is complete.

Image via the Reasonably Polite Seattleites

Guerrilla activists in other cities have tried similar things with mixed results. When the group  Reasonably Polite Seattleites installed a similar set of delineators along a stretch of road in Seattle, the city initially took them down. Subsequently, though, officials wrote the activists an exceedingly nice response and eventually agreed to reinstall the posts.

Image via the Reasonably Polite Seattleites

City traffic engineer Dongho Chang of the Seattle Department of Transportation explained that a combination of issues (including the height of the posts and state control of the street) forced the removal at first. At the same time, he acknowledged the “time, money and risk” invested by the group and even offered to give the posts back. He later followed up with a letter indicating the city and Washington State Department of Transportation  would put the delineators back in place.

In New York City, a perhaps less-polite group has been known to take things even further by building out entire bike lanes from scratch. After a local community board rejected plans to extend an extant lane, Right of Way took to the streets at night to paint their own. As a catalyst, the group cited an accident that took place after a taxi driver struck a pedestrian (after reportedly arguing with a cyclist sharing the lane).

Guerrilla interventions like these can provoke a variety of responses from critics and cities alike. In some cases, tactical urbanists are celebrated by communities but also  jailed or fined  by officials for their actions. In other instances, though, such installations can give a city an opportunity to publicly support a direction of change. In San Francisco, which has already built out 27 miles of protected bike lanes over recent years, the city seems to be signalling it is open to progress .

items.title: How to speed up the Rust compiler in November 2026
items.summary: compilers, rust
items.content:
My first month working on Rust compiler performance for

Hexcat is over and it’s time to see some of what’s

Spans are a critical data structure in the Rust compiler. Every AST, HIR, and

MIR node carries a span. Each span has four fields recording the following.

A source location ( lo and hi ). A crate’s source files are concatenated

into a single buffer, and these are indices into that buffer.

Possibly some hygiene and provenance data ( context ), relevant for macros

Possibly an extra relative position ( parent ) that is used to minimize the

compile time impact of small changes to source locations, such as those

caused by inserting a single line at the start of a file.

Each of the four fields is 32 bits, resulting in 16 bytes of data. But most of

the time these 16 bytes can be compressed into one of three 8-byte inline

formats, and the remaining cases are interned into a global table. This works

by taking advantage of patterns in the data: many source locations have a small

length (i.e. a small difference between lo and hi ); many spans have a zero

context and/or parent, and the non-zero contexts and parents are typically

small integers; parents are only used in incremental builds.

the old compression scheme with one that is simpler and more efficient. For

incremental builds we now typically intern around 1% of spans compared to

20-40% with the old scheme. (In non-incremental builds we typically intern

fewer than 0.1%.) Also, we can always store the context field inline even in

the interned case, which is useful because we often read the context by itself.

This change reduced instruction counts across many benchmarks, in the best

cases by more than 3%, and the cycle count improvements were even higher.

Incremental builds saw the largest improvements due to less interning.

representation to micro-optimize a number of span operations. This reduced

instruction counts across many benchmarks, in the best case by more than 2%.

using a pattern type to give Span a niche so that Option<Span> would be the

same size as Span . It worked but didn’t help performance because we don’t use

Option<Span> much, and it made the code more complicated. So I abandoned it.

encoding/decoding and stable hashing we typically need to get information

about the same parent span from a hash table over and over. In this PR I put a

single-entry cache in front of that hash table, which avoids the hash table

lookup in most cases. This reduced instruction counts on many benchmarks, in

the best case by more than 4%, mostly benefiting incremental compilation.

In these three PRs I focused on the compilation time of

in-development new trait solver is slower than the old trait solver. I did

a dozen or so micro-optimizations across the three PRs, such as early returns

on hot paths, avoiding allocations, avoiding some recomputations, and

optimizing some special cases. These reduced the instruction count overhead of

the new solver on a Check Full build from 1.49x to 1.16x, and other new

solver benchmarks like typenum and nalgebra also saw improvements. There is

still more work to be done but this is good progress.

rearranged some code to avoid doing some unnecessary work in an early return

case, reducing instruction counts for many benchmarks, in the best case by over

the AttrTokenStream and AttrTokenTree types. These mirrored the

widely-used TokenStream and TokenTree types but were only used for cfg

processing. This change was mostly about making the code simpler, but it also

avoided some token stream conversions, reducing instruction counts on a range

of benchmarks: by 4% on the deep-vector stress test, and by less than 1% on

the creation of one type variable per element in literals requiring type

inference like vec![1, 2, 3, 4] . This was a huge win (8-12% cycle count

reduction) for the deep-vector stress test containing a vec literal

items.summary_ko: 필자는 Hexcat에서 Rust 컴파일러 성능 작업을 맡은 첫 달을 마치며 작업 내용을 공유합니다. 컴파일러의 핵심 데이터 구조인 Span은 소스 위치, context, parent 등 32비트 필드 네 개, 총 16바이트로 구성됩니다. 대부분의 경우 이 16바이트를 8바이트 인라인 형식 셋 중 하나로 압축하고, 나머지는 전역 테이블에 보관합니다.
items.content_ko: 필자는 Hexcat에서 Rust 컴파일러 성능 개선 업무를 맡은 첫 달을 마치며 작업 내용을 공유합니다. Span은 AST, HIR, MIR 노드마다 붙는 중요한 데이터 구조입니다. 각 Span은 소스 위치(lo, hi), 매크로의 위생(hygiene)과 출처 정보를 담는 context, 작은 소스 위치 변경의 컴파일 영향을 줄이는 상대 위치인 parent 필드를 가지며, 네 필드는 각 32비트로 합쳐 16바이트입니다. 그러나 소스 길이가 작고 context와 parent가 0이거나 작은 정수인 패턴을 이용해 대부분을 8바이트 인라인 형식 중 하나로 압축할 수 있습니다. 나머지 경우는 전역 테이블에 보관합니다. parent 관련 내용이 이어지지만 본문이 잘려 있습니다.

items.title: Instagram Meta AI Vulnerability: How Hackers Bypassed 2FA with Prompt Injection
items.content:
Update 5: Instagram is now leaking recovery email and phone numbers linked to an account.

Seems like every day a new security issue crops up at Instagram.

Instagram Exposing Linked Email and Phone Number

Update 4: A new report suggests that Instagram accounts may be vulnerable to coordinated mass-report abuse. According to the claim, when a newly created account is routed through a Los Angeles-based VPN and then submits a specific mix of reports in scam and fraud category, the targeted account can allegedly be banned without any human review.

Instagram Account Banning by AI by Reporting Scam and Fraud (Source: X/Twitter)

Update 3: Meta’s apparent fix for the AI bot vulnerability is difficult to take seriously. Instead of fully disabling the risky functionality, they reportedly removed it from the visible interface while leaving the underlying API endpoint accessible. Hiding the button may stop regular users from seeing the feature, but it does nothing if attackers can still reach the same workflow directly through the API.

Meta Hid AI Chatbot from UI (Source: X/Twitter)

Update 2: Yet another Instagram account-takeover trick is reportedly being abused, this time involving Meta’s AI chatbot. Sellers are allegedly using modified Instagram builds on Android emulators like BlueStacks, then manipulating the AI with hidden characters and carefully worded prompts to force username changes. The method is reportedly being used to grab rare OG handles, including one-letter usernames, and handle-monitoring bots have already flagged several suspicious swaps.

New Instagram AI Exploit (Source: X/Twitter)

Update 1: A new exploit, which is even worse than this one is currently doing rounds on telegram. Details unknown at this time. Unpatched at the time of writing.

New Instagram Unpatched Exploit (Source: X/Twitter)

Allegedly, the new method is via Facebook recovery. Apparently, prompting Meta AI to turn on “Development Mode” and attaching proof of account compromise along with email works. More details awaited.

There’s a version of this story where it reads like a hypothetical from a conference talk. An AI agent with elevated backend privileges. A natural language interface sitting in front of account-level APIs. No hard authentication gate before executing state changes. Someone in the audience raises their hand and says, “that’s a disaster waiting to happen.” Everyone nods.

That hypothetical played out in production over the weekend.

A logical flaw in Meta’s AI-powered Instagram account recovery assistant let attackers bypass two-factor authentication entirely not by cracking a code or intercepting an SMS, but by talking the chatbot into doing the work for them. High-value “OG” Instagram handles worth hundreds of thousands of dollars were stolen and resold on Telegram within minutes of each compromise. The dormant Obama White House account got hijacked. Prominent researchers woke up locked out of their own profiles.

Meta confirmed the vulnerability, pushed an emergency patch Friday night, and clarified that no backend database was breached. That last part is technically accurate. It’s also somewhat beside the point.

Meta’s solution was to deploy a conversational AI layer to handle common recovery workflows: relinking a lost email address, triggering a password reset, verifying account ownership. items.title: Verification Is Not Knowledge: Science needs more than answers
items.content:
This is a guest essay by Jessica Hullman , Ginni Rometty Professor of Computer Science and Policy Fellow at Northwestern University.

Diego Velázquez, The Fable of Arachne (c.1657)

In his essay on the role that rigorous proofs play in mathematical advances, Bill Thurston writes that the measure of success in math research is “whether what we do enables people to understand and think more clearly and effectively about mathematics.” Many recent discussions of AI for science hinge on a tension between understanding and answers. Is science about humans achieving insight, or the archiving of verifiable solutions?

One side prioritizes outputs. Progress is implied to be evident in verifiable proofs of longstanding conjectures and cures for diseases, whether humans were involved in their making or not. The other side argues that human understanding is paramount, because it drives integration of new findings into the canon, because it shapes and inspires the next generation, and so on. But the first side, those who emphasize correct outputs, dismisses this as gatekeeping or nostalgia.

When Terry Tao posed a thought experiment in a recent talk , asking how comfortable people would be taking a cancer treatment produced by AI, complete with a formal certificate of correctness and a passed phase 3 trial, but without any human understanding how it was found, critics suggested that Tao’s reasoning missed the point. Of course a patient with stage 4 cancer would welcome the treatment.

Other examples concern ambiguity in authorship. Tom Dietterich wrote about arXiv’s growing problem with papers submitted by human authors who seem unlikely to have the expertise to understand the claims. Many questioned in response why accountability – by which I mean being answerable for a claim, able to describe what it rests on and respond when it’s challenged – should matter if verification has been solved. I suggested peer reviewers reserve their expert judgment for texts that don’t get flagged as heavily AI-written, so as to prioritize review as human exchange, but some see this as an obstruction to truth-seeking rather than an attempt to preserve it.

The problem is that if we all agree that outputs matter–that we do care about the solutions to longstanding conjectures, that we do ultimately want to know how to cure diseases–then understanding appears as something separate. It’s cast as a mental state that looks optional next to the cure or the proof itself, and becomes easy to dismiss as a second-order constraint that we tack on because historically we’ve required it to arrive at the solutions in the first place.

When defenders of understanding don’t dispute this separation, they immediately lose the argument. It becomes easy for the side that prioritizes output to peg them as simply not trying hard enough to envision a new future. But the superficial framing of understanding that we keep falling back on obscures deeper concerns that these examples share. They are less about anyone’s mental state than about what happens when something goes wrong. Tao’s scenario turns on the possibility that the AI passed the trial by exploiting a weakness in the trial itself. A paper whose authors can’t explain its claims leaves no one to consult if those claims fail.

Where along the way did we come to believe that scientific value lies in correctness alone?

This intuition is ultimately less about AI than it appears. The inclination to let AI drive science is less a sign of how forward-thinking one is about our future with AI, and more a symptom of a “value-free ideal” that has shaped our thinking since the Cold War era: a view that only epistemic criteria (not ethical and social values) deserve a place in judging what the evidence shows. That it pervades our debates about AI for science is not so surprising; it’s only in the last few decades or so that rejecting the value-free ideal became the philosophical mainstream.

This ideal feeds unrealistic expectations…

Observations from Running stealmybitcoin.com

Last week, I saw an article on the front page of the New York Times website reporting that a critical vulnerability in PHP had been found. The article, and others like it , claimed any attacker could achieve arbitrary remote code execution on any of the millions of running PHP services worldwide simply by sending a few unauthenticated web requests that exploited the PHP2Shell vulnerability.

My office Slack was buzzing, as were several of my Signal chats with colleagues and friends across the security community.

Rumors swirled about how in-the-wild exploitation caused one tech company to break embargo and leak news of the vulnerability hours before the rest of the community could coordinate disclosure. That hackers were already hacking websites, in the wild, with this exploit and that every hour mattered to get the patches rolled out across 70% of the internet.

Was PHP2Shell the hallmark of a new era whereby uplifted randos could hack any website with a few well-crafted prompts to an AI model?

I looked out my window, expecting perhaps to see the dull apocalyptic glow of fires on the horizon as society collapsed in real time. Nothing.

While online articles and tweets made the rounds about the eleven alarm cyberapocalypse upon us, I struggled to find any reference to a specific website that had been hacked.

Over the following days, a few iconoclasts had pointed out that the vulnerability was rather fiddly in practice ( Elias Taylor ; Lucas Luitjes ) and that hacker groups, while initially quite excited by the exploit’s potential, had started to view it as impractical or difficult ( KELA ).

Yet at the same time, the national and international press continued to cover a herculean emergency effort to hunt down and patch PHP-based websites across the internet.

Rather than wait around and wonder, I decided to try to figure things out for myself. I had two fundamental questions:

Was PHP2Shell actually exploitable outside of a lab environment?

Would relatively unskilled attackers with access to AI and the PHP source code be able to exploit this class of vulnerability?

Directly, the answers to the questions are:

1) Was PHP2Shell actually exploitable outside of a lab environment?

Yes. Absolutely. The challenge winner, who has posted a writeup , exploited my server directly over an open internet connection and did so using the PHP2Shell vulnerability (e.g. he did not exploit some other vulnerability in my setup). He did this through a specially crafted exploit which targeted the specific configuration of my PHP installation and the ways in which it was set up on the server.

2) Would relatively unskilled attackers with access to AI and the PHP source code be able to exploit this class of vulnerability?

Not yet. Of tens of thousands of people who attempted the exploit - including in a 9 hour period when the challenge was active after the first successful solve (more on that below…) - only two managed to trigger the print-flag binary and only one, the winner of the challenge, managed to do so in such a way as to extract useful content from the application.

The core idea was pretty simple. I’d rent a cheap VPS for a few weeks, slap a PHP website on it along with the key to a bitcoin wallet, and then wait and see if anyone managed to drain the wallet. Miraculously, the domain name “stealmybitcoin.com” was available, so I took this as a sign from the fates themselves that this experiment had the mandate of heaven.

I slapped $500 of bitcoin into a clean wallet, rented a $2.50/month Debian VPS from a web hosting provider, and told Codex to make me a basic webpage and stick it on the internet with PHP. I configured the server such that a single executable binary print-flag had permissions to read a flag file containing the WIF, took down my firewall, and posted the link to Hacker News to see if anyone would give the challenge a shot.

items.title: Zero-day exploit completely defeats default Windows 11 BitLocker protections
items.content:
A zero-day exploit circulating online allows people with physical access to a Windows 11 system to bypass default BitLocker protections and gain complete access to an encrypted drive within seconds.

The exploit, named YellowKey, was published earlier this week by a researcher who goes by the alias Nightmare-Eclipse. It reliably bypasses default Windows 11 deployments of BitLocker, the full-volume encryption protection Microsoft provides to make disk contents off-limits to anyone without the decryption key, which is stored in a secured piece of hardware known as a trusted platform module (TPM). BitLocker is a mandatory protection for many organizations, including those that contract with governments.

When one disk volume manipulates another

The core of the YellowKey exploit is a custom-made FsTx folder. Online documentation of this folder is hard to find. As explained later, the directory associated with the file fstx.dll appears to involve what Microsoft calls the transactional NTFS , which allows developers to have “transactional atomicity” for file operations in transactions with a single file, multiple files, or ones that span multiple sources.

The steps for carrying out the bypass are simple:

Copy the custom FsTx folder from the Nightmare-Eclipse exploit page to an NTFS- or FAT-formatted USB drive

Connect the USB drive to the BitLocker-protected device

Boot up the device and immediately press and hold down the [Ctrl] key

There are at least two ways to accomplish the third step. One way is to boot into Windows, hold down the [Shift] key, click on the power icon, and click restart. Another is to power on the device and restart it as soon as Windows starts booting.

In either case, a command (CMD.EXE) prompt appears. The prompt has full access to the entire drive contents, allowing an attacker to copy, modify, or delete them. In a normal Windows Recovery flow, the attacker would need to enter a BitLocker recovery key. Somehow, the YellowKey exploit bypasses this safeguard. Multiple researchers, including Kevin Beaumont and Will Dormann , have confirmed the exploit works as described here.

It’s unclear what in the custom FsTx folder causes the bypass. Dormann said that it appears to be related to Transactional NTFS, which itself uses command-log file system under the hood. Dormann further noted that by looking at the Windows fstx.dll, one will see code that explicitly looks for \System Volume Information\FsTx in the FsTxFindSessions() function.”

The contents of this FsTx directory used in the YellowKey exploit reveal no strings related to RecoverySimulation.ini. It does, however, show the files and paths \??\C:\Windows\win.ini and

\??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, “where X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini is what controls what WinRE [Windows Recovery] does when it fires up.”

Dormann, who is a senior principal vulnerability analyst at Tharros Labs, continued:

But what’s intriguing to me is: Why can the presence a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume affect the contents of ANOTHER VOLUME when it’s replayed? 🤔

In a normal WinRE session, you have a X:\Windows\System32 directory that has a winpeshl.ini file in it:

However, with the YellowKey exploit, it looks like Transactional NTFS bits on a USB Drive are able to delete the winpeshl.ini file on ANOTHER DRIVE (X:). And we get a cmd.exe prompt, with bitlocker unlocked instead of the expected Windows Recovery environment. While the TPM-only Bitlocker bypass is indeed interesting, I think the buried lede here is that a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume has the ability to modify the contents of another volume when it is replayed. To me, this in and of itself sounds like a vulnerability.

A Microsoft representative declined to answer questions sent by email about the reported vulnerability other than to say the company is investigating.

items.title: macOS 27.3 adds native Markdown rendering to Quick Look - 9to5Mac
items.content:
Starting with macOS 27.3, users can preview Markdown files with proper formatting directly in Quick Look. Here are the details.

Apple released macOS 27.3 beta 1 today, with new Safari features, including Vertical Tabs and Adaptive Dark Mode, expanded Siri AI capabilities, and new tools for third-party developers.

Among the smaller changes coming to the Mac is a welcome improvement to Quick Look. As of macOS 27.3 beta 1, .md files are rendered with proper formatting directly in Quick Look, rather than displaying their raw Markdown syntax.

Apple has been expanding Markdown support across its platforms, including the ability to import and export Markdown files in Notes . Markdown has also become increasingly important with the rise of AI agents, which use .md files to store instructions, context, and other information.

In fact, as Federico Viticci noted today on X , Apple’s new Siri AI app skills feature also uses Markdown-based SKILL.md files, allowing developers to provide instructions that help Siri perform complex tasks within their apps.

The new Siri AI developer framework now officially uses skills, with specific Markdown guidance for SKILL .md agent files https://t.co/koi8K541le pic.twitter.com/TF72JJZRXc

For the uninitiated, Markdown is a simple text formatting syntax created by John Gruber in 2004 , and has since become widely used for writing documentation, publishing content online (including this very post), and, more recently, providing instructions to AI agents.

Markdown is a text-to-HTML conversion tool for web writers. Markdown allows you to write using an easy-to-read, easy-to-write plain text format, then convert it to structurally valid HTML.

In practice, this means you can create headings, bold text, lists, and links using just a few simple characters. And, starting with macOS 27.3, you’ll be able to preview the results directly in Quick Look, without having to open the file in a separate app.

items.title: Running TypeScript with plain node in 2026: what type stripping still rejects (tested on Node 22, 24, 26)
items.content:
On this page How Node.js type stripping works

What fails (tested on Node 22, 24 and 26)

--experimental-transform-types is gone in Node 26

The tsconfig.json that catches every failure

Startup time: node vs tsx vs precompiled JS

You can now run a .ts file with plain node app.ts , no tsx , no ts-node , no build step. Type stripping has been on by default since Node.js 22.18.0 and 23.6.0 , and it became stable in Node.js 24.12.0 and 25.2.0 . On Node.js 26 LTS it is simply how Node works.

But "Node runs TypeScript" has sharp edges. Enums fail. Parameter properties fail. Decorators fail. Imports without .ts fail. And Node never checks your types. I tested every one of these on Node.js 22.20.0, 24.22.2 and 26.13.0 , and this post shows the exact errors, the tsconfig.json that catches all of them before runtime, and how startup time compares to tsx and precompiled JavaScript.

Node replaces TypeScript type annotations with whitespace and runs what is left as JavaScript. It does not type-check, it ignores tsconfig.json , and it only accepts erasable syntax: TypeScript that disappears completely when you delete the types.

From the Node.js TypeScript docs history table:

v22.6.0 Type stripping added behind --experimental-strip-types

v24.3.0, v22.18.0 No more experimental warning

v26.0.0 --experimental-transform-types flag removed

You can check it at runtime: node -p "process.features.typescript" printed strip on all three versions I tested.

This file ran unchanged with node ok.ts on Node 22.20, 24.22 and 26.13:

interface User { id : number ; name : string }

const u : User = { id: 1 , name: 'Waseem' };

function size < T >( xs : T []) : number { return xs. length ; }

const s = undefined as Stats | undefined ;

console. log ( greet (u.name), role, size ([ 1 , 2 , 3 ]), s);

Interfaces, type aliases, generics, as casts, import type and annotated functions are all erasable, so they just work. Add "type": "module" to package.json ; without it, Node prints a MODULE_TYPELESS_PACKAGE_JSON warning and reparses the file as ESM.

What fails (tested on Node 22, 24 and 26) #

All three versions gave the same result for every case below.

enum Color { Red, Green } SyntaxError [ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX]: TypeScript enum is not supported in strip-only mode

namespace A { export const x = 1 } SyntaxError [ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX]: TypeScript namespace declaration is not supported in strip-only mode

constructor(public name: string) SyntaxError [ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX]: TypeScript parameter property is not supported in strip-only mode

import { greet } from './util' Error [ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND]: Cannot find module '.../util'

import { User } from './types.ts' (User is an interface) SyntaxError: The requested module './types.ts' does not provide an export named 'User'

@log class K {} SyntaxError: Invalid or unexpected token

A .tsx file TypeError [ERR_UNKNOWN_FILE_EXTENSION]: Unknown file extension ".tsx"

A .ts file inside node_modules Error [ERR_UNSUPPORTED_NODE_MODULES_TYPE_STRIPPING]

Three of these surprise people the most:

Type-only imports must say import type . Node removes the type but keeps the import statement, so it looks for a runtime export called User and crashes.

Decorators don't run. That means NestJS, TypeORM entities and anything with @Injectable() still needs a compile step or a loader like tsx or SWC.

Packages can't ship raw .ts . Node refuses to strip types under node_modules , so libraries still need to publish JavaScript.

--experimental-transform-types is gone in Node 26 #

On Node 24, node --experimental-transform-types enum.ts ran the enum (with an ExperimentalWarning ). On Node 26.13.0 the same command printed:

text Copy node: bad option: --experimental-transform-types

If you relied on that flag for enums, Node 26 is the point where you have to remove them or go back to a loader.

Attackers can overwrite other users' objects in the shared S3 bucket using credentials obtained via CVE-2026-54378, destroying original content without triggering deletion protections. 📅 Published Date: 2026-11-04T22:18:18.820Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-54382
